title: Moving the taller wall inward
summary: Keeping the shorter wall fixed while moving the other wall inward shrinks width without raising the water-level cap, so capacity cannot increase.
context: On ht = [3, 8, 5, 2, 7, 7, 3, 4], starting from i = 0 (shorter wall 3) and j = 7 (taller wall 4) with capacity 21, move the right taller wall one step inward while keeping the left shorter wall fixed to see why capacity cannot improve.
description: Left pointer i stays at 0 (height 3), while right pointer j moves left from 7 to 6 (height ht[6] = 3, returning wall 7 to unselected gray). The light-blue water region narrows to span indices 0 to 6 at height 3, captioned below "Moving the taller wall inward always reduces capacity" and "Current capacity: cap = min(3, 3) × (6 - 0) = 18".

frames.title: Moving the taller wall inward
frames.explanation: Changing the right wall from height 4 to height 3 keeps water height at min(3, 3) = 3 while shrinking width from 7 to 6, dropping capacity from 21 to 18 as a local comparison.

result: Extending this reasoning: with shorter wall i = 0 fixed, replacing j with any index from 1 to 6 keeps water height at most 3 across a strictly smaller width, so none can beat 21. Although the figure draws only j = 6, all pairs keeping i = 0 are ruled out on the same grounds, justifying moving shorter wall i instead.
